faq.q: Can FeNO replace spirometry in diagnosing asthma?

faq.q: What if a FeNO analyser is not available?

exam: A 25‑year‑old with intermittent wheeze has FeNO 45 ppb. What is the next step? — Start low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid and arrange repeat FeNO in 4 weeks.
How does smoking affect FeNO interpretation? — It lowers FeNO, potentially masking eosinophilic inflammation; consider clinical picture.
When would you choose a biologic over increasing inhaled steroids? — Persistent FeNO > 50 ppb despite high‑dose ICS/LABA, with frequent exacerbations.
What distinguishes allergic asthma from COPD using FeNO? — Elevated FeNO (> 35 ppb) supports allergic asthma; COPD usually shows normal or low FeNO.
A child with atopic dermatitis has FeNO 30 ppb but normal spirometry. What does this suggest? — Subclinical eosinophilic airway inflammation; monitor and consider early ICS if symptoms develop.
Why might FeNO be falsely high in a patient using a wood‑fire stove? — Ambient NO from biomass combustion can raise measured FeNO.
What is the clinical relevance of a decreasing FeNO trend after starting therapy? — Indicates effective suppression of airway eosinophilia and good treatment response.
In a resource‑limited hospital without FeNO, how would you assess eosinophilic asthma? — Use peripheral eosinophil count, symptom pattern, and response to a short trial of inhaled corticosteroid.
ai.title: Exhaled Nitric Oxide in Respiratory Medicine
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) is a non‑invasive marker of airway eosinophilic inflammation, useful for diagnosing and monitoring asthma, especially where sputum or bronchoscopy are unavailable.

b: Measured in parts per billion (ppb) with an approved handheld analyser
sections.p: FeNO measures the concentration of nitric oxide in a patient’s breath, reflecting type‑2 (eosinophilic) airway inflammation.

t.b: Is airway eosinophilia present? – Values ≥ 35 ppb in adults (≥ 25 ppb in children) suggest eosinophilic inflammation; lower values make it unlikely.

b: Low: < 25 ppb – unlikely eosinophilic asthma
Intermediate: 25‑35 ppb – borderline, consider clinical context
High: > 35 ppb – active eosinophilic inflammation
sections.p: FeNO does not stage disease but helps gauge inflammation intensity and response to anti‑type‑2 therapy.

b: Allergic asthma – the commonest cause in low‑resource settings
Atopic dermatitis or allergic rhinitis with airway involvement
Helminth infections (e.g., schistosomiasis) that drive eosinophilia
Smoking reduces FeNO – a low result may mask inflammation
sections.p: Elevated FeNO is most often due to allergic or eosinophilic asthma, but other conditions can raise levels.

b: Recurrent nocturnal cough
Exercise‑induced dyspnoea
Rapid symptom relief after inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) initiation
sections.p: Patients usually present with wheeze, cough, and variable airflow limitation that improves with bronchodilators.

b: Spirometry – confirms reversible obstruction
Peak flow diary – tracks variability
Allergy testing – identifies triggers
sections.p: FeNO complements clinical assessment and spirometry, especially where sputum eosinophils cannot be obtained.

t.b: Is airflow obstruction present and reversible? – FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 with ≥ 12 % improvement after bronchodilator confirms asthma.
What atopic triggers exist? – Positive wheal ≥ 3 mm supports allergic asthma.
Is systemic eosinophilia present? – Count ≥ 0.3 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ supports type‑2 inflammation.

b: Repeated oral corticosteroid courses
Hospital admission for status asthmaticus
Progressive decline in lung function
sections.p: Very high FeNO alone is not a red flag, but uncontrolled eosinophilic inflammation can lead to severe asthma attacks.

b: Low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) – first‑line to suppress eosinophils
Add long‑acting β₂‑agonist (LABA) if symptoms persist
Consider leukotriene receptor antagonist when adherence to inhaler technique is poor
Biologic anti‑IL‑5 or anti‑IL‑4Rα agents for FeNO > 50 ppb despite high‑dose ICS
sections.p: Treat the underlying eosinophilic inflammation first, then optimise bronchodilator therapy.

b: Target FeNO < 25 ppb in adults
Educate on trigger avoidance (dust, smoke, biomass fuel)
Ensure correct inhaler technique
sections.p: Repeat FeNO after 4‑6 weeks of therapy to assess response; use trends rather than single values.

b: eCO reflects smoking exposure, not airway inflammation
Sputum eosinophils require laboratory processing not always feasible
sections.p: FeNO is sometimes mistaken for exhaled carbon monoxide (eCO) or sputum eosinophil count.

b: Current smoking lowers FeNO – a low result may hide eosinophilia
Recent use of high‑dose oral steroids suppresses FeNO
High ambient NO (e.g., indoor biomass burning) can falsely raise values
sections.p: Factors that alter FeNO independent of asthma can give false‑high or false‑low readings.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness with peak flow < 50 % predicted
Repeated need for rescue inhaler > 4 times daily
